analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from making or enforcing non-compete agreements for hourly and lower-paid workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in July 2021, was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to void existing non-compete agreements for certain non-exempt employees and bar employers from entering into, enforcing, or threatening to enforce new ones for those workers. Non-competes can prevent lower-wage workers — in fields like retail, food service, and staffing — from taking a better job at a competing company, cutting off a key route to a raise. The bill preserves trade-secret protections, so employers could still restrict the sharing of confidential information, and it does not affect higher-paid workers outside the FLSA's overtime exemption. It also gives the Department of Labor enforcement authority, with civil penalties against employers who violate the ban.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 30 million workers earning under about $35,000 per year (those eligible for overtime under FLSA rules) who would no longer face non-competes that trap them in jobs and block them from taking competing offers that come with better pay.

how_it_helps.text: For workers with non-competes, the bill voids existing agreements and bars new ones, so those workers could freely take a higher-paying job with a competitor instead of staying trapped in a lower-paying role.
The bill preserves trade-secret law, meaning employers keep protection against theft of genuine confidential information like formulas, customer lists, or proprietary software.
The bill gives the Department of Labor wage-and-hour enforcement power over non-competes, so violations carry civil penalties rather than requiring the worker to hire a lawyer and file suit.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in low-wage sectors who use non-competes to keep turnover low and wages suppressed — including retail chains, staffing agencies, and franchise operators — would lose a tool for retaining workers at below-market pay.

drawbacks.text: The bill only protects FLSA non-exempt employees, so it leaves in place non-competes for higher-paid and salaried workers who often have more specialized skills and face similar restrictions.

Employers could still rely on other restrictive covenants like non-solicitation agreements, which limit a worker from bringing clients or coworkers to a new employer and can function much like a non-compete in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the benefit is substantial and direct: freedom to take a competing job without legal threat. The cost to employers is the loss of a retention tool they used to hold down wages, which is precisely the point of the bill, though the narrow scope (FLSA non-exempt workers only) limits how far the benefit reaches.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in July 2021, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 117th Congress adjourned in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Marco Rubio introduced the bill on July 15, 2021, with Sen. Maggie Hassan as an original cosponsor, framing it as a worker-freedom measure that bridges party lines.
The bill was referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, which is the standard first stop for labor legislation.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor debate — appears in the bill's record for the rest of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use non-competes to hold lower-wage workers in place — including retail chains, call centers, and staffing firms — are better off, since the restriction on their practice never became law and those agreements remain enforceable. Workers are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers using non-competes; workers remain restricted

industries.industry: Retail, food service, and other low-wage service-sector employers
industries.note: These employers commonly use non-competes for hourly workers to reduce turnover and hold wages down; the bill would strip that tool, and the industry's gain from stopping the bill comes at the direct expense of workers' mobility and pay.
Staffing agencies and franchise systems often use non-competes to lock workers into placements or franchises, and the ban would remove that leverage over vulnerable workers.
